subject: Fysik
title: Sound, light and the universe
sourceSummary: Sound waves and how we perceive pitch and volume, the propagation of light, reflection and refraction, and basic facts about the solar system and the vast distances in the universe.

questions.opener: Think about what happens in the air when something vibrates, for example a guitar string.
choices: Light that moves in waves
Pressure waves that spread through a medium, for example air, when something vibrates
An electrical signal in the air
A vacuum moving forward
questions.explanation: Sound arises when something vibrates and sets the particles in a medium (e.g. air) oscillating, which creates pressure waves that spread outward and reach the ear. Sound is not light and needs a medium in order to spread.

questions.prompt: What determines pitch (whether a tone sounds high or low)?
questions.opener: Think about how fast something vibrates.
choices: The speed of sound
The frequency, that is, how many oscillations per second the sound source makes
How loud the volume is
The distance to the listener
questions.explanation: Pitch is determined by frequency, measured in hertz (Hz) — more oscillations per second gives a higher tone, fewer oscillations gives a lower tone. Volume, on the other hand, is controlled by the amplitude of the sound wave (the size of the oscillation), not by frequency.

questions.prompt: Why do you hear thunder after you see lightning, even though they happen at the same time?
questions.opener: Compare how fast light and sound each travel through air.
choices: The sound is created later than the lightning
Light travels much faster than sound, so light from the lightning reaches your eye almost instantly while the sound takes longer
The ear is slower than the eye at reacting
Lightning is quieter than thunder
questions.explanation: Light travels at about 300,000 km/s while sound only travels at about 340 m/s in air. That's why light from the lightning reaches us almost instantly, while the sound (thunder) lags behind and is heard later, especially if the distance is large.

questions.prompt: What is it called when light bounces off a surface, for example a mirror?
questions.opener: Think of the word for when something is "bounced back".
choices: Refraction
Reflection
Absorption
Diffraction
questions.explanation: Reflection means that light bounces back from a surface, for example a mirror. Refraction, on the other hand, is when light changes direction as it passes between different media (e.g. air and water).

questions.prompt: Why does a straw in a glass of water appear to "bend" at the water's surface?
questions.opener: The light changes medium (air to water) and this changes its speed and direction.
choices: The straw is actually bent
The light refracts (changes direction) as it goes from air to water because it changes speed in the different media
The water magnifies the image evenly along the whole straw
The eye cannot perceive straight lines underwater
questions.explanation: Light travels at different speeds in air and water, and when the light crosses the boundary between the media it changes direction — this is called refraction. This makes the straw look shifted or "bent" at the water's surface, even though it is actually straight.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a star and a planet?
questions.opener: Think about whether the celestial body produces its own light or not.
choices: Stars are always smaller than planets
A star produces its own light and heat through nuclear reactions, while a planet only reflects light from a star
Planets are always warmer than stars
There is no real difference
questions.explanation: A star, like the Sun, generates energy through nuclear reactions in its core and therefore shines with its own light. A planet, like Earth, has no light source of its own but is visible because it reflects light from a star it orbits.

questions.prompt: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. Light from the next-nearest star takes about 4 years. Explain what this says about distances in the universe, and why astronomers use light-years as a unit of distance.
questions.opener: Compare how far light, the fastest thing we know of, travels in such different amounts of time.
questions.answer: The fact that starlight takes minutes in one case and years in the other shows that distances in space are enormously larger than distances on Earth — even at light's incredible speed (about 300,000 km/s), it takes years to reach us from other stars. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, and it is used as a unit because ordinary measures like kilometres would give unreasonably huge and unwieldy numbers for distances between stars and galaxies.
steps: The Sun is our nearest star, and its light takes only 8 minutes to reach Earth.
The next-nearest star is so much farther away that its light takes about 4 years to reach us.
Light is the fastest thing we know of (about 300,000 km/s), yet the journey takes years — this shows how enormous the distances in the universe are.
Measuring such distances in kilometres would give extremely large, unwieldy numbers.
That's why light-years (the distance light travels in one year) are used as a practical unit of distance in astronomy.

questions.prompt: Summarise the basic concepts of sound, light and the universe.
questions.opener: Go through sound, then light, then space before turning the card over.
questions.answer: Sound: pressure waves that spread through a medium (e.g. air) when something vibrates, requires a medium in order to spread · Frequency (Hz) determines pitch — more oscillations per second gives a higher tone · Amplitude determines volume/loudness · The speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s, much slower than light's roughly 300,000 km/s · Reflection: light bounces back off a surface, e.g. a mirror · Refraction: light changes direction when it changes medium, e.g. from air to water · The solar system: the Sun is a star that shines with its own light via nuclear reactions, the planets (including Earth) orbit the Sun and only reflect light · The universe: contains countless stars and galaxies, and the distances are so enormous that they are measured in light-years (the distance light travels in one year).
